title: The government shutdown ends after President Trump signs the budget bill into
description_short: The government shutdown ends after President Trump signs the budget bill into law, marking the end of the longest shutdown in American history
description_medium: On November 12, 2025, Trump signed a funding package that reopened the federal government after a 43-day shutdown, the longest in U.S. history at the time. The House passed the measure 222–209 after an agreement between Republicans and centrist Senate Democrats. It funded the government through January and provided full-year funding for some agencies. The deal also reversed federal layoffs and restored employee pay and food services.
description_long: President Trump signed the funding bill on November 12, 2025, ending a 43-day federal shutdown. CNN reported that the House passed the package 222–209 after negotiations between Republicans and centrist Senate Democrats. The agreement funded the government through January and provided full-year funding for some agencies, while reversing federal layoffs carried out during the shutdown. Reopening allowed paychecks to resume for federal employees and restored critical food and nutrition services relied on by tens of millions of people. The shutdown was the longest in U.S. history at that point. Trump described the agreement as a political victory and accused Democrats of trying to extort concessions; that characterization was his own account of the dispute, not a neutral description of the negotiations. The record establishes the end date and immediate budgetary effects, but does not include the full bill text or the subsequent funding outcome after January. This entry documents the resolution and the administration’s role in signing it without treating either party’s rhetoric as a settled explanation for why the shutdown lasted.

title: Denies Puerto Rico Hurricane Death Toll
description_short: Trump claimed the Hurricane Maria death toll in Puerto Rico was inflated, disputing official estimates after a major study pegged deaths near 3,000.
description_medium: Trump disputed Puerto Rico’s Hurricane Maria death toll on September 13, 2018, calling the estimate of nearly 3,000 deaths inaccurate and claiming Democrats had inflated the number. The estimate came from a major study commissioned by the Puerto Rican government after the storm. His statements challenged the documented scale of deaths from the disaster and were criticized by officials and researchers. This entry records the denial, not a change to the official count.
description_long: On September 13, 2018, Trump publicly rejected the estimate that Hurricane Maria had caused nearly 3,000 deaths in Puerto Rico, asserting that Democrats had made up the figure to damage him politically. The estimate followed a major study commissioned by the island’s government to account for deaths associated with the storm, including people whose deaths were not immediately recorded as hurricane-related. The Guardian report linked to this entry documents Trump’s claim and the dispute over the count. The statement did not revise Puerto Rico’s official estimate or provide an alternative mortality study. It instead cast doubt on the figure and attributed it to partisan motives. Death toll estimates after a major disaster can change as researchers account for indirect deaths and gaps in records, but that general uncertainty does not support describing a study’s estimate as fabricated. This entry records the president’s denial and the basis of the disputed count without treating his assertion as evidence that the number was invented.

description_short: An Illinois judge ruled that Trump should be removed from the state’s Republican primary ballot under the 14th Amendment, with the decision stayed pending appeal.
description_medium: An Illinois judge ruled on February 28, 2024, that Trump should be removed from the state’s Republican primary ballot under Section 3 of the Fourteenth Amendment, which bars certain officeholders who engaged in insurrection from holding office. The ruling was stayed while Trump appealed, so it did not immediately remove him from the ballot. The U.S. Supreme Court later reversed state-level disqualification efforts, leaving Trump eligible in Illinois.
description_long: On February 28, 2024, an Illinois state judge ruled that Donald Trump was ineligible for the Republican primary ballot under Section 3 of the Fourteenth Amendment. That provision disqualifies certain people who, after taking an oath to support the Constitution, engaged in insurrection or rebellion. The judge’s order was stayed pending appeal, so it did not take effect immediately and Trump remained on the ballot during the review. In March 2024, the U.S. Supreme Court held that states could not enforce Section 3 against federal candidates on their own, reversing the state disqualification effort. The CNBC report linked to this entry covers the Illinois ruling. This sequence matters because the headline describes a trial-level decision, not a completed removal from the ballot. The record concerns a constitutional eligibility ruling and subsequent review; it does not describe an election official independently excluding Trump or establish a criminal conviction for insurrection.
